overview.text: Standard deviation is a measure of how spread out values in a data set or probability distribution are around their mean. It is the nonnegative square root of variance: because variance averages squared deviations from the mean, standard deviation summarizes that spread while returning it to the data’s original units. A small standard deviation means values tend to cluster near the mean; a larger one signals more variation, though unusually extreme values can increase it substantially. For a whole population, the usual symbol is σ; for a sample, s is commonly used, and its calculation uses n−1 rather than n. It helps describe variability, but is not a complete picture of a distribution.

key_facts.text: Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance; it is zero when all data values are equal.

To calculate it, find deviations from the mean, square them, average the squared deviations using the appropriate population or sample formula, then take the square root. The population formula divides by N; the sample formula divides by n−1.
σ commonly denotes population standard deviation, while s denotes sample standard deviation.
Standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data; variance is expressed in squared units.
Extreme values in distribution tails can greatly affect standard deviation; for long-tailed data, measures such as the median absolute deviation or interquartile range may be more stable.
